25 Years Since the Anthrax Attacks: Where Are We Now?

October 7, 2026 • 4:30 – 5:30 pm EDT

Video On Demand

Hosted by The CSIS Bipartisan Alliance for Global Health Security

Sophia Hirshfield: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome. I’m Sophia Hirshfield, an associate fellow with the Global Health Policy Center here at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. It has been 25 years since a series of letters containing anthrax powder were distributed through the U.S. Postal System in an act of bioterrorism. In the weeks following the fateful attacks of September 11th, 2001, letters containing a powdery form of anthrax were mailed to several major news media outlets and the offices of two U.S. senators. Amid the uncertainty and fear surrounding these attacks, an estimated 32,000 people across Florida, New Jersey, New York, and Washington, D.C., received preventative antibiotics. Twenty-two people became infected, five of whom eventually died. Dozens of buildings were contaminated with anthrax spores, with decontamination efforts taking several years and costing hundreds of millions of dollars. The ensuing FBI investigation to find who mailed the anthrax letters became one of the largest and most complex in the history of law enforcement. And much is still unknown about the motivations and origins of these attacks. During today’s conversation we will not only reflect on how the United States responded to the anthrax attacks 25 years ago, but how that experience motivated much of our foundational bio defense infrastructure. We will explore current U.S. efforts and capabilities to deter future bioterrorist attacks, identify and attribute attacks accordingly, and mitigate their impacts on the health and wellbeing of Americans. Our conversation today will be moderated by CSIS senior advisor Major General Paul Friedrichs, Dr. Friedrichs served as the inaugural director for the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response, and prior to that held several senior biodefense roles at the White House and the Pentagon. He’s also the senior biopreparedness fellow at RAND, and an adjunct professor of surgery and preventive medicine at Uniformed Services University. Our first panelist is former North Carolina Senator Richard Burr, who is a principal policy advisor and chair of the Health Policy Strategic Consulting Practice at DLA Piper, and a co-chair of our CSIS Bipartisan Alliance for Global Health Security. During his nearly three-decade career across both the House and the Senate, Senator Burr was instrumental in authoring and advocating for landmark biodefense and pandemic preparedness legislation, including the Pandemic and All Hazards Preparedness Act, or PAHPA.We’re also joined today by Stewart Simonson, a senior advisor to the Global Health Policy Center who served in key leadership roles at the Department of Health and Human Services, including during the 2001 federal anthrax response. He has also served seven years as assistant director general for general management at the World Health Organization and five years as the WHO representative to the United Nations. He’s currently a senior advisor with Global Health Strategies. And finally, we’re very pleased to welcome Dr. Wendi Kuhnert, deputy director for laboratory readiness and response at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases. Dr. Kuhnert began at the CDC in 2001, has held roles in the Division of Viral Hepatitis and National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases. And today, her team is responsible for monitoring, identifying, and preparing for high-consequence biological threats. Before we begin, I’d like to thank Steve Morrison, Michaela Simoneau, Caitlin Noe, Priya Chainani, Emily Wilson, and our exceptional CSIS streaming and broadcasting team for their support in pulling this event together.And without further ado, please join me in welcoming our panelists, as I turn it over to Dr. Friedrichs to get the conversation started. (Applause.)Paul Friedrichs: Thank you, Sophia, for that introduction. And I’ll echo the thanks to our CSIS team, and to all of you who are joining us. And I also want to give a thanks to the Gates Foundation, because they are helping to make this possible today. They recognize the value of partnering with CSIS. And we’re grateful for that, and hope that that will continue. If you’ll indulge me, I’m going to start for a moment making sure that we understand what we’re talking about. We’re talking about Robert Stevens, an editor at The Sun. We’re talking about Thomas Morris, a postal worker who, along with his colleague Joe Curseen, worked at the facility that handled the anthrax letters. We’re talking about Kathy Nguyen, who worked in a hospital in New York City whose mail happened to be adjacent to one of the anthrax letters. And Ottilie Lundgren, a 78-year-old resident of Oxford, Connecticut. And for the life of me, I still can’t find a compelling explanation for how her mail got mixed up in this. Letters were sent to Tom Brokaw at NBC, to Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle. And in case you’ve forgotten, 24 of his staff actually tested positive for anthrax after the letter was open in his office. Senator Patrick Leahy, multiple other New York post offices, and, as we heard, 32,000 people were eventually treated for possible exposure to anthrax as a result of this attack. It’s also worth noting that we still don’t have an agreed-upon explanation for who did this. We settled a multimillion-dollar claim from one researcher who we said very publicly was culpable for this, and then retracted that. Another researcher who was identified as a person of interest committed suicide. And there were extensive reviews of that investigation, which highlighted opportunities to improve our ability to attribute a biological attack. In this day and age, when the media is filled this week with reports on a death at a lab in Russia, which may or may not have been plague, may or may not have been many things, it’s a great reminder that biological threats are a real concern, and will continue to be so. This administration has published their compliance report, which highlights that both Russia and North Korea have bioweapons programs. There are multiple indications of growing natural biological threats as well as accidental leaks, which should lead us to look back at what happened 25 years ago and ask ourselves, what did we learn from this and are we better prepared today than we were before? And I want to start, Senator Burr, with you. You know, I’ve been in combat many times, and that was, oddly enough, often less fraught than going in front of Congress. (Laughter.) But you were always very gracious, sometimes very pointed. And you’ve played such an incredibly important role in this space. Could I ask you to start setting the stage a little bit from your perspective as someone who was on the Hill and very influential afterwards in learning from this?Richard Burr: Well, let me also thank the Gates Foundation and Steve for doing this. What I’ve learned in the United States Senate is – or, Congress – is memories are very short. And to recognize something that happened 25 years ago is challenging for people with our color hair, to remember all the aspects of it. But I think the thing that stood out the most was what we weren’t prepared for. And that’s not to say that we responded quickly, from an investigative standpoint. It was really a medical response to a crisis. But it took months, if not years, for us to begin to think about, how do we change this so that’s not the situation that we’re in next time? And I think that’s what was initiated out of this. It initiated partnerships between the federal government and academia, partnerships between the federal government and companies, all targeted at what was stimulated by anthrax. And that’s an overall review of what were we capable of doing and, in a perfect world, how would we have done it differently? I think Stu would agree that we’re still learning things that we didn’t pick up 25 years ago in that review with every incident that we see. And I think the thing that scares me the most is we’re headed into a period where attribution is going to be much more difficult, with AI-designed pathogens that really don’t – they don’t contain the DNA that we are accustomed to looking at, and tracking, and assigning responsibility to.So, as I’ve shared with you privately, I’m always scared when there’s not an incident in the United States for an extended period of time where most people are happy, because it takes Congress having some type of fear of something for them to actually appropriate and to enforce the right behaviors. Unfortunately, we’re at that point, I think, both in research and in commitment, that not all of the entities that are responsible are getting the funding and the support they need. Dr. Friedrichs: Well, let me also thank the Gates Foundation and Steve for doing this. What I’ve learned in the United States Senate is – or, Congress – is memories are very short. And to recognize something that happened 25 years ago is challenging for people with our color hair, to remember all the aspects of it. But I think the thing that stood out the most was what we weren’t prepared for. And that’s not to say that we responded quickly, from an investigative standpoint. It was really a medical response to a crisis. But it took months, if not years, for us to begin to think about, how do we change this so that’s not the situation that we’re in next time? And I think that’s what was initiated out of this. It initiated partnerships between the federal government and academia, partnerships between the federal government and companies, all targeted at what was stimulated by anthrax. And that’s an overall review of what were we capable of doing and, in a perfect world, how would we have done it differently? I think Stu would agree that we’re still learning things that we didn’t pick up 25 years ago in that review with every incident that we see. And I think the thing that scares me the most is we’re headed into a period where attribution is going to be much more difficult, with AI-designed pathogens that really don’t – they don’t contain the DNA that we are accustomed to looking at, and tracking, and assigning responsibility to.So, as I’ve shared with you privately, I’m always scared when there’s not an incident in the United States for an extended period of time where most people are happy, because it takes Congress having some type of fear of something for them to actually appropriate and to enforce the right behaviors. Unfortunately, we’re at that point, I think, both in research and in commitment, that not all of the entities that are responsible are getting the funding and the support they need. Stewart Simonson: Thank you, Paul. Let me say that from the beginning I had no interest at all in biodefense and public health preparedness. I came to HHS with Secretary Thompson. I came part time, beginning February 2nd of ’01. And then on August 20th, I started full time. He said I had no choice. I had to come over to – I had to come over to the department. He said, what kind of job do you want? I said, well, I’d like to be one of the deputy general counsels. I had been his legal counsel in Wisconsin. And he said, all right, you can be the deputy general counsel for public health. It was interesting. On the day I started, he said, there is one additional responsibility that I would like you to have. You did it in the governor’s office, and I’d like you to do it here. You’ll be responsible for emergency management, and working with law enforcement, and so forth. And that’s what I did in the governor’s office. And I said, well, thank you. I appreciate your confidence. But I don’t want to do that. You never get a good night’s rest in emergency management. It is always something. And he said, Stu, be reasonable. It’s HHS. How much can there be? (Laughter.) So on September 13th, I was – 12th and 13th I was in New York. And we realized then there was no real infrastructure in the Office of the Secretary for emergency preparedness and response. What is called ASPR today did not exist. There was no operation center on the sixth floor. There was really nothing in HHS headquarters to support the secretary in his decision-making responsibilities. So I started to cobble together something, beginning on September 12th. Recruited D.A. Henderson, who had been the dean of the Hopkins School of Public Health, to come in as an advisor. He had written, with Dr. Parker and others, a consensus paper on how to manage the medical consequences of an anthrax attack. That was in 1989, and he’d updated it a few times. But he was a very accomplished and able man, and an inspirational leader. He came in part time, and eventually, before the anthrax letters, became director of what we call the Office of Public Health Preparedness. But it really wasn’t an office. It was bolted onto the Office of General Counsel. And in fact, D.A. and I shared an office. There really wasn’t much. So on October 4th, we heard about Mr. Stevens. Then we said, well, maybe it is naturally occurring. It does happen. And then we heard about another person at American Media, I think it’s called, someone who worked in the mailroom. It was very clear at that point that it was deliberate, but whether it was terrorism, as we’ve come to think of it today, or just something else, a murder, still. So maybe good to step back a bit and say that the attack came in two waves. The first wave was the American Media hit, and –Dr. Friedrichs: And that’s American Media the company, not American media, the enterprise. Mr. Simonson: That’s true. And the CBS and – or NBC.Dr. Friedrichs: NBC, yeahMr. Simonson: The New York hit. I think the New York Post also. That wave was with a type of anthrax that was crude. It clumped and didn’t aerosolize particularly well. The second wave was with a highly purified form of anthrax that aerosolized very well. In the meantime, as between these two attacks, we were trying to figure out what it was that we knew about anthrax. And it really wasn’t all that much. It’s veterinary disease – cows die of it, horses die of it – but not a lot of human cases. Maybe 10 in the last hundred years. And so we’re trying to figure out, well, how to predict the response. No one knew, for example, how clean was clean. If a site was hit with anthrax, how to disinfect it and decontaminate it? It wasn’t clear. So Peggy Hamburg, who had been the assistant secretary in the Clinton administration – and she had been really at the forefront of preparing the country for a biological event. The Clinton administration did an awful lot to prepare the U.S. for anthrax and other biological events. We had all the countermeasures that were available then. We never had a problem with countermeasures that were licensed. We had – there were some gaps, but we had a fair amount of antibiotic and vaccine. So I asked Dr. Hamburg to convene scientists to help us understand anthrax. And so she was at the Nuclear Threat Initiative at the time. And she brought together everyone who knew anything about anthrax, people who had worked in the offensive program, the 1969 – pre-1969 program. There were many, many people there, and it was very interesting. But what was clear was that there wasn’t a lot of rock-solid information that we could rely on. And I remember very specifically as we were talking about the Post Office – this was before the two postal workers were affected – we asked, well, will the Post Office, will the mail system be compromised by this? And the answer was based on what we know, and based on the material that the U.S. made in the pre-’69 program, they didn’t think so. And I have a very clear recollection of Dr. Fauci saying, do you mean that the that the postal workers are not at risk? And they said – these were people who had worked with the organism – based on what we know, we don’t think so. But that was based on the cruder form of the organism. And it turned out that between the first and second wave, and the second wave was all in Washington – they, he, whoever did it, purified it very significantly, to the point that the folks who were looking at it under the electron microscope were surprised. They had never seen anything like it. And these were people who were experienced with this out of the Army Medical Research Institute. So trying to determine how to respond to this was a real challenge at HHS, because there was no culture of working with law enforcement. And even within HHS, there wasn’t a lot of information sharing between the CDC and the Office of the Secretary. This is what ultimately led to the Office of Public Health Emergency Preparedness, which later became ASPR, with the objective of serving as the secretary’s planning and analytic arm for a biological, nuclear, chemical event. It was never, back then, contemplated as an operating division. It was purely a planning and analytics. And as a result, we didn’t know what they were finding at these various laboratories. And eventually we got a lot more clarity on it. And Tom Ridge had been appointed the director of the Office of Homeland Security, and he brought a lot of, I think, coordination and clarity to it. But what I learned in all of this, and it informed the next five years for me, was, first of all, when it comes to the life sciences, and infectious disease maybe in particular, there’s a lot we don’t know. Even diseases that have been around for time immemorial, a lot we don’t know. And you have to be very humble in approaching it. And I never heard Dr. Henderson or others in our office talk about anything with certainty. It was always, well, this is what we know. The other thing I learned is how important it is to have a culture that can work vertically within the department, but also with the interagency community. And that is an enormous challenge. And particularly with law enforcement and intel. That was not within the culture of HHS, CDC, NIH. There was no history of that. We had one secure phone, that we could never quite get to work, in the secretary’s office. So that was something that was addressed in what became ASPR. I had maybe five or six former FBI agents, police, just to have that sort of connection. The CDC did the same thing. And so I don’t think today you would find any of that disconnect with the law enforcement and intel community. And I think the final thing is that countermeasures matter. Development of new countermeasures is essential to stay ahead of this. We had, I said, thanks to Dr. Hamburg and President Clinton, we had plenty of doxy and cipro, and we had plenty of a 1970s-approved vaccine. We had no therapeutics, right? Once the spores began to germinate, there was no way to deal with that toxin. You either lived or you died. Thanks in large part to Tony Fauci, we began developing what we call extra-regulatory approaches, what we would do in a general emergency. And for example, at the NIH we set up a plan to run plasmapheresis clinics to four soldiers who had been – an airman and Coast Guardsmen – who had been immunized against anthrax, to get those antibodies and try to use that as passive therapy. Today we have three therapies, I believe, in the stockpile. At least we had. Two monoclonal antibodies and old-fashioned and highly dependable anthrax immunoglobulin. But we still have the 1970s vaccine. And that’s something that has to be addressed. I have to say, though, we tried. There were a lot of mistakes made by me, in particular. And we failed. That vaccine – was called the recombinant protective antigen vaccine – never made it even into trials. There was a lot of politics in that too, because the minute that vaccine went into trials and looked to be developing toward licensure, the current maker of the approved product got engaged. And so what was – what they were not satisfied with at HHS they litigated on Capitol Hill. And that’s something you can’t win in a government agency, at least not an agency that I worked in. So those are my lessons. Dr. Friedrichs: And, Stu, you’ve covered a lot of ground there. And one of the things –Mr. Simonson: In 10 minutes? (Laughter.)Dr. Friedrichs: Give or take a little bit. And I think, you know, one of the things that you touched on was ASPR. And I just want to publicly recognize the members of Congress, in particular Senator Burr, because you played such a crucial role in the legislation that authorized the creation of ASPR. Can you – before we go to Dr. Kuhnert, can you say just a couple of words about that? Senator Burr: Yeah, because it actually started as something very different. There was a recognition that in a full-fledged emergency response, and we’d seen this with some other things that had happened in the meantime, that to initiate that response had to involve the White House, and it had to involve the Oval. So the original legislation had the vice president of the United States serving in the role that ASPR ended up as a job description. And it was Vice President Cheney who, when he read the legislation, he said, hell no. (Laughter.) And we went back to the drawing board, and that’s where we created the ASPR inside of HHS. Mr. Simonson: He wasn’t so bashful behind the scenes, I’ll tell you. (Laughter.)Senator Burr: Well, I will say this, that when President Trump won, the administration assigned the vice president – if you remember, he was on Air Force Two when he got the call as it related to COVID. I actually called the vice president and said, this is how it was supposed to work. Mr. Simonson: Exactly. Exactly.Senator Burr: And I think it took about six days before the microphone was taken out of his hand, which was an important aspect of the executive branch bringing the American people up to date for a very brief period every day in the afternoons. And he was doing a great job of it, until it became a two-hour event. And that’s where they sort of lost the trust – the interest of the American people. Dr. Friedrichs: And I will say, and you had one final legislative action related to this that helped shape where we are today in the movie, and that was the creation of OPPR. So could you say a few words about that? Senator Burr: Well, I was glad you were over there. Dr. Friedrichs: I haven’t forgiven you, by the way. (Laughter.)Senator Burr: Listen, it was a natural thing, given how the architecture looked at the time, that these were decisions that needed to be assessed and a plan put together inside of the White House. And any other construction of this would not work. And I think, regardless of what this administration does in its last two years, the next administration will reinstate the power of that component too. Because it’s a critical component to our ability to determine the risk and respond to it. Dr. Friedrichs: And I think both of you are touching on a truth that hopefully is evident to everybody in the room and online, and that’s that while this may start as a public health discussion, when people are sick, it quickly becomes a discussion that moves into the economic space, and the national security space, and the political space. And you can’t – you can’t ignore that reality. And –Senator Burr: Well, Stu danced around this, but he said it. He did it diplomatically.Dr. Friedrichs: As he always does. Mr. Simonson: (Laughs.)Senator Burr: Is what we learned was agencies don’t work well with other agencies. You know, government is stovepiped, like a lot of other things. And it’s simply because the power in Washington is determined by the size of a budget. And you’re not going to share. Even though you might – I might be aided by what you can provide to this issue at any given point in time, you’re going to want some budget to do it. And I’m not going to want to give it up. So I’m going to try to concentrate that in my bucket, so Congress doesn’t take money away. Dr. Friedrichs: And I think, you know, that waxing and waning nature of our political system changes all the time, as you said. It’ll change from one administration to the next. But biology doesn’t change that much. And that’s where CDC comes into this discussion. And very glad that you’re here, Wendi, because CDC played an important role. And in fact, you know, I went back and I reread – and for those of you who haven’t looked at it in a while, there’s a really good report from the GAO from 2004 that critiqued the CDC. And it was quite complimentary. They highlighted excellent communication, a real effort to put facts out, what we knew and what we didn’t know. So, Wendi, maybe you could share a little bit from inside the CDC of what you all reflect on what happened 25 years ago, and where you are today. Wendi Kuhnert: OK, I’ll try to do that. It’s a challenging subject. I think for us, we actually look at it starting in 1999, because I think, to the point of diagnostics, we didn’t have one in 1999. You know, we were doing culture. We were doing very basic technologies. And I guess there was some forethought. And we did work on a molecular test. It was PCR at the time. That was the state of the art. Not anymore. You know, so I think we were lucky to have that test when we did. I think there’s probably a lot of other things we could say we didn’t have, but I was glad we actually had a test. And I think that was really important, and was really critical to the diagnosis for some of those cases. I think – to the struggles that you’ve pointed out, I think the environmental testing, the ability to screen environmental surfaces, I think that – you know, that existed then, and, unfortunately, I think it still exists now. That is one of the gaps that we still recognize. But one of the things I tried to think about as I looked back over the last 25 years is what have we done? And I tried to think about it in four different buckets of work. And the first bucket was thinking about our laboratory capacity. You know, we still do have world-renowned anthrax experts. You know, I think the funding maybe isn’t what it should be, but we still do have the staff. And I think that’s been a real highlight of the agency and our ability to maintain that expertise over time. We have also really focused on the laboratory response network. And it doesn’t test for everything. It does still test for anthrax, and it tests for a number of other biothreat agents. And it is really a very unique laboratory network that includes environmental testing, military labs, veterinary labs, and, obviously, the public health labs. So I think that’s pretty critical. Within CDC, we have looked at our ability to move our diagnostics forward. And I think with the initiative, the Advanced Molecular Detection, we’ve worked really hard to help push forward molecular technologies for both CDC as well as the public health sector, in a way that I – we were losing ground about 10 to 12 years ago, and I think we’ve improved. And then, finally, I think the legislation for the Select Agent Program. And I think we haven’t mentioned that, but I think that’s really important for how we look at the biosecurity and biosafety of managing these pathogens, knowing where they’re at. Again, not perfect, but I think it’s really been a move forward over the last 25 years. I think we’ve done a lot with diagnostics. Am I worried that we still have a long ways to go? Yes. I think there are concerns with, you know, the biosecurity and the way these pathogens can be engineered. I think that is scary. But I think for now, for some of the most basic tests, I think our advanced molecular detection has come a long way. We have tried at CDC to work on data modernization. And I think the newest initiative, the Biothreat Radar, I am hopeful that that will really bring a lot of these things together and will help us move forward with – you know, from a data consolidation and a surveillance perspective, to bring all these things together. Medical countermeasures was already brought up. I think we have a number of things for anthrax. We still have a ways to go with that. I think it’s also important that what we learned then was something we had never done before, and I think we’ve gotten better at it over the last 25 years. But it’s mass dispensing and producing the clinical guidance. Those were things we had never really done before, you know, especially at that scale. So I think that’s important. I also think we’ve worked on coordination. Something that I hadn’t thought about until thinking about today is we didn’t have an emergency operation Center in 2001. The first EOC at CDC was in 2003. And now it’s everywhere. It’s a term that’s, you know, all over the world. So I think that’s – for me, it’s pretty interesting to think back, like, what did we do? You know, as I sit and look at where we are now with our Ebola response, and looking at, you know, how we bring people together for that, it had to have been a real struggle to manage that response even internal to just CDC without that that coordination. So I think that’s really important. I do think CDC has worked hard at our communications. And we’ve developed a number of mechanisms to be able to speak more clearly, but also faster, and to be able to convey some of this in a little bit more timely fashion than I think we were doing at the time. So I think that’s maybe where I’ll pause for now. I know there’s probably additional questions, but that’s kind of my thoughts on the last 25 years. Dr. Friedrichs: Well, thanks. And, before we open it up to the audience for questions, I just want to pull out a couple more threads that several of you have touched on here. So, you know, we’ve talked about what happened 25 years ago, and what we’ve learned from it, and we can’t ignore the elephant in the room. There was a COVID pandemic. It affirmed we still had work to do in the testing space. And I think you’ve spoken to some of the things that CDC continue to learn after that, and to improve on with that. All three of you have touched on the need to continue to fund biosurveillance, to continue to fund research, to continue to fund communication platforms, and how to communicate. And also, and Wendi, you touched on this, we need to continue to fund and improve our ability to distribute countermeasures during an event. And that’s really critical. When we talk about lessons learned from what happened 25 years ago, lessons learned from what happened six years ago, and, as we’re seeing now with Russia, you know, there’s an approach to every outbreak that starts with very common themes. So let’s start with biosurveillance. You had mentioned environmental surveillance as an area for improvement. So we have had BioWatch. And we’ve had a variety of projects. I’m excited that ARPA-H is working on the BREATHE program now, and is coming up with a successor to that. I think that’s really good news there. You had mentioned AMD. That’s another real step forward in bringing new technologies into the biosurveillance space. Sir, you had mentioned attribution. And given that we’re talking about deliberate attacks, can you say a couple more words about that? Because it would be a mistake, I think, for anyone to assume that because we’re not perfect, somehow that means that we’re an attractive target. Senator Burr: Well, this is – I don’t get too deep into it, because I’m going to have to put my intelligence committee hat back on, and I tend not to go there. The reality is that the first is the medical response, but the second has to be, who did this. And who could be a naturally occurring, or it could be intentional. But that’s absolutely crucial, from the standpoint of what the next steps after that are. And I think as we talk about AI engineered, AI directed, we begin to lose the fingerprints that have, at least historically, been there to suggest, well, we need to look at this region of the world, or we need to look at this particular group. And we really are going to be in a situation where we’ll have an architecture that addresses the most important thing, which is response. But everything that we tried to build up to this point happens in that total architecture. And I think we saw it in real time in COVID. We haven’t reauthorized PAHPA, which was the – which was the architecture. And I think one of the reasons, Stu, that we got better over time, was we had certain things that happened during that five-year period that we were smart enough to reflect in the reauthorization of the bill. Which said, hey, maybe we don’t need the president to be the one to trigger emergency use. Maybe we should let the secretary do it, because we can’t get the president’s attention. And that was a real life experience that we went through. Dr. Friedrichs: That’s right. Senator Burr: So we changed it over three different iterations, or four different iterations. And that’s why it’s a workable architecture today. But we haven’t affected the changes in the last five years, which incorporates all of COVID. And it certainly doesn’t take into account the advances that have been made from a technology standpoint that should be incorporated in that architecture, because it may expand collaboration between agencies. It may suggest the areas that Congress needs to fund. And so I really see PAHPA reauthorization is a crucial component to our ability to not just respond, but to understand how to address everything thereafter. Dr. Friedrichs: Well, and, you know, having just been in China with Dr. Morrison and others, I think it’s interesting that others view our approach to this, this very holistic approach, as a different way that they seek to understand. And I think this has been one of our real strengths.
